name: Hair loss concealing hat/cap

lead: Caps, hats and beanies cover thinning areas or baldness, so the scalp and hairline are hidden straight away and you get a neater, more confident look. Styles are chosen to suit the face and outfit.
The hat physically covers the scalp, so the effect is visible while worn. It leaves the underlying hair unchanged.

paras: People wear them day to day, picking fits and styles that match their clothing and face shape. They are often used alongside treatments or while waiting on hair-loss results.
Tight or compressive headwear worn for long periods is associated with traction alopecia.

web.title: Can Wearing a Hat Make You Go Bald?

angle.text: Caps, hats and beanies are worn to cover thinning hair or baldness, so the scalp is hidden straight away and the head looks neater. Users pick styles that suit their face and outfit. The effect is visible while worn and does not treat the hair loss.

lead: Caps, hats and beanies are worn to cover thinning hair, a receding hairline or a bald crown, giving an immediate change in how the head looks without any treatment. People choose them for the instant coverage and because a cap can also frame the face and add a style element.[1][2] Wikipedia lists hats alongside comb-overs, wigs and toupees as ways to hide hair loss.[1]

Headwear covers hair loss rather than altering the hair growth cycle. Wikipedia notes that the psychological impact of hair loss varies; two meta-analyses of men with androgenetic alopecia found distress on average to be moderate, and balding men were no more likely to have depression or self-esteem problems than non-balding men.[1]

A widely repeated belief holds that wearing hats causes baldness. Dermatologist John Anthony of the Cleveland Clinic says the research is limited: two twin studies did not link hat wearing to worse thinning, and one found less temple hair loss among daily hat wearers. He adds that very tight or hot hats might reduce blood flow or put tension on follicles.[2] Wikipedia notes that tightly pinned caps and compressive helmets can cause traction alopecia, a mechanical loss distinct from androgenetic baldness.
infobox: Traction alopecia from tight or pinned headwear [2]

paras: Headwear is a non-medical way to hide a receding hairline or crown thinning. Options include baseball caps, beanies, flat caps and similar styles, and it sits among other concealment methods such as restyled hair, wigs and toupees.[1] It does not change the hair growth cycle.

Cleveland Clinic dermatologist John Anthony says research is limited, that hair loss usually stems from genetics, hormones, age and medical conditions, and that two twin studies did not link hat wearing to worsening thinning.[2] He suggests a loosely fitting option may be a safer bet than a tight cap, and says tension-related loss could be temporary at first but permanent over time if it continues.[2]

Wikipedia reports that headwear can cause traction alopecia when it pulls on hair for long periods, including caps pinned tightly at the side or back of the head and tight helmets used for cycling, motorcycling or skiing; it is mechanical rather than hormonal and the main treatment is stopping the tension. Anthony also names itchy or inflamed scalps from a hat as a concern.[2]
No studies found on hats as hair-loss concealment. Two twin studies on hat wearing and hair thinning have been described by a dermatologist, who reported no link to worsened thinning.[2]
